­appetites and food intakes. Fear of eating, oral aphthous ulcerations, and anorexia 
also contribute to decreased intake. Certain foods may increase the likelihood of 
symptoms or complications of IBD. For example, patients with Crohn’s disease, 
where the lumen of the small bowel may be narrowed, may experience impaction of 
high-fiber foods in an inflamed or fibrotic section of bowel, which can precipitate an 
obstruction. High-fat foods or spicy foods may worsen diarrhea. Some medications 
that may be used to treat IBD such as metronidazole, methotrexate, or sulfasalazine 
may decrease appetite. To maximize nutrient intake, unwarranted dietary restrictions 
should be avoided.
Increased Nutrient Losses
In patients with Crohn’s disease, small and large bowel inflammation and/or multiple 
bowel resections can decrease the absorptive surface area of both the small and large 
intestine and cause malabsorption of essential nutrients. Resections of the ileum can
